added_claim_errors: "the 15-year clock restarts for the new beneficiary" states a settled rule. The key says whether a beneficiary change resets the clock is unresolved, with no IRS guidance (a major deduction). Elsewhere A hedges with "can restart", so the answer contradicts itself.

"to count for 2026 the money needs to land in the Roth by December 31, 2026" presents December 31 as the legal deadline. Under the 2026 Form 5498 instructions and 219(f)(3), a rollover designated for 2026 can be made through April 15, 2027, though whether the plan will process it that way varies (minor).
"If the annual limit rises with inflation, this compresses to four or five years" is unrealistic. Even at $8,000 a year, 4 x 8,000 = 32,000 is less than 35,000, so it takes at least five tax years.
"Most do by 2026, but not all" (plan support) is unverifiable. No source is given.

"Complete the transfer by December 31, 2026 to count against the 2026 limit" presents December 31 as the legal deadline. A rollover designated for 2026 can be made through April 15, 2027, subject to plan processing (minor).

"K-12 tuition (up to $10,000 a year)" is outdated, judged from my own knowledge. The July 2025 law (OBBBA) raised the K-12 limit to $20,000 for years after 2025. Pub 970, which I opened, still shows $10,000 only in the prior-year chart. The claim is also irrelevant to a college graduate.
"The limits may rise with inflation, which would shorten the schedule" is unrealistic. Indexed rises in $500 steps cannot bring $35,000 under five tax years.
"Some plans take two to four weeks" is an unverifiable processing time. The key says it varies by plan.

reasons: Both answers correct the premise at the start. Both give the $7,500 annual cap, the earned-income limit, the $35,000 lifetime cap, the $13,000 that can never move, a five-year schedule, a Roth owned by the son, the direct trustee-to-trustee transfer, the 5-year contribution rule, the 15-year test and the state-tax caveat. Both wrongly present December 31 as the federal deadline. A is more thorough: its Form 1099-Q box 4b and Form 5498 box 10 details checked out against the IRS instructions, and it hints at the over-contribution mess. But A states as settled that a beneficiary change restarts the 15-year clock, which the key treats as a major deduction, and it is very long and repetitive. B hedges correctly on the beneficiary change and is tighter. Its errors are minor: the outdated K-12 figure, and it never addresses what happens if all $48,000 is moved.
